title: Law of Definite (Constant) Proportions — Statement, Examples and Limitations
notes: The second law of chemical combination: Proust's law of definite proportions with its classic percentage data, the calculations it supports, and the compounds that break it.

'A chemical compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed proportion by mass, regardless of its source or method of preparation.' Established by Joseph Proust (1799) against Berthollet, who believed composition could vary continuously with conditions.
• Water: from river, sea, rain or synthesised from H₂ + O₂ — H : O = 1 : 8 by mass (11.1% H, 88.9% O).
• Carbon dioxide: 27.27% C, 72.73% O (C : O = 3 : 8) whether from burning carbon, respiration or limestone decomposition.
• Copper oxide: 79.9% Cu, 20.1% O whether prepared by heating copper in air or reducing CuO in hydrogen.

A pure compound has a fixed formula (H₂O, CO₂, CuO): fixed atom counts and fixed atomic masses give a fixed mass ratio — a direct consequence of Dalton's theory (the law was actually strong evidence *for* atoms).
• Percentage composition: % element = (mass of element in formula ÷ molar mass) × 100.
• Mass of element in a given sample: sample mass × (%/100) — e.g. oxygen in 90 g of water = 90 × (8/9) = 80 g.
• Purity analysis: a brass sample or an ore is assayed by comparing its metal percentage with the theoretical value for the pure compound.
1. **Non-stoichiometric (berthollide) compounds:** Fe₀.₉₃O, FeS₁₋ₓ, Cu₂₋ₓO — composition varies within a small range; the law needs a true formula compound.
2. **Isotopic variation:** D₂O (heavy water) has H : O = 2 : 8, not 1 : 8 — the same 'compound' differs when isotopes change.
3. **Mixtures, solutions and alloys** vary continuously in composition — the law is for pure compounds only.
4. Polymers and associated molecules with variable chain length have no single fixed composition.
confusion: ❌ The law means elements always combine in the same proportion. ✅ It applies to a given *compound*; the same two elements may form several compounds (CO, CO₂) with different ratios — that is multiple proportions.
❌ Heavy water is a counterexample to chemistry being consistent. ✅ It shows the law depends on the isotope chosen — D₂O and H₂O are different compounds.
❌ The law applies to brass or steel. ✅ Alloys are mixtures with variable composition; only pure compounds are covered.

summary: Proust's law of definite (constant) proportions, established in 1799, states that a pure chemical compound always contains the same elements combined in the same fixed ratio by mass, regardless of its source or method of preparation — water from rain, river or synthesis always contains hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1 : 8. The law follows from a pure compound having a fixed formula, so its atom counts and atomic masses are constant, and it underpins percentage-composition, mass-of-element and purity or assay calculations. Its real limits are the non-stoichiometric (berthollide) compounds such as Fe₀.₉₃O, isotopic variants such as D₂O, and mixtures or alloys whose composition varies continuously.
importantConcepts: Proust's law: a fixed mass ratio of the elements in a pure compound, independent of its origin
Percentage composition, % element = (mass of element in the formula ÷ molar mass) × 100
A fixed formula as the microscopic reason for constant composition
Non-stoichiometric (berthollide) compounds such as Fe₀.₉₃O, FeS₁₋ₓ and Cu₂₋ₓO
Isotopic substitution, where D₂O gives H : O = 2 : 8 instead of 1 : 8
Variable-composition systems — alloys, mixtures and solutions — that fall outside the law
importantStatements: The law of definite proportions was established by Joseph Proust in 1799, against Berthollet's view that composition could vary with conditions.
Water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1 : 8, that is 11.1% hydrogen and 88.9% oxygen.
CO₂ always contains 27.27% carbon and 72.73% oxygen by mass, so C : O = 3 : 8.
CuO is always 79.9% copper by mass, whether prepared by heating copper in air or by reducing CuO with hydrogen.
The law applies to a given compound; the same two elements may form several compounds with different fixed ratios, as CO and CO₂ do.
Non-stoichiometric compounds such as Fe₀.₉₃O and Cu₂₋ₓO vary in composition within a range and have no single percentage.

keyPoints: A pure compound has fixed composition, independent of source or method of preparation.
H : O in water is always 1 : 8 by mass.
Berthollet believed composition could vary continuously; careful analysis of natural and artificial carbonates settled the debate in Proust's favour.
The law is a consequence of a fixed formula, not an independent fact.
Always say 'proportion by mass' — volume ratios belong to Gay-Lussac's law.
specialNotes: D₂O (heavy water) contains hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2 : 8, not 1 : 8, because the isotope changes the atomic mass; D₂O and H₂O are therefore different compounds.
Berthollides such as Fe₀.₉₃O and Cu₂₋ₓO have no single fixed formula, so no single percentage composition applies to them.
Alloys, mixtures and solutions vary continuously in composition; the law covers pure compounds only, so brass and steel are outside it.
Polymers and associated molecules with variable chain length have no single fixed composition either.
examShortTricks: Always include the source-independence clause in the statement — that clause carries the marks.
Memorise two ratios: H : O in water is 1 : 8 and C : O in CO₂ is 3 : 8.
Mass of element in a sample = sample mass × (percentage ÷ 100), so 90 g of water contains exactly 80 g of oxygen.
To separate the two laws: definite proportions = one compound, multiple proportions = a pair of compounds of the same two elements.
examNotes: Usually a 2–3 mark statement question followed by a one-mark numerical on percentage composition.
A frequent 5-mark question asks for a comparison with the law of multiple proportions using CO and CO₂.
Limitations are commonly asked as a follow-up; quoting Fe₀.₉₃O and D₂O secures full marks.
Assay and purity questions use the law as a reference percentage for the metal content of ores and alloys.
